Model 2: Condition-Specific Models

Sections 5.7 and 5.8 implemented in ten reviewable steps

Author

Analysis Team

Published

August 2, 2026

Mission — model-2

Model 1 answered the question “what predicts absence among Canadian workers?” Model 2 asks it seventeen more times, once inside each chronic-condition subgroup, which is what Sections 5.7 and 5.8 request. It is a self-contained estimation script: it reads the Ellis parquet, builds its own frames, runs its own selection, and persists its own evidence. Nothing in it is loaded from model-1.

What it does borrow from model-1 is shape. The same ten steps, the same artifact roles — t6 is the deliverable table, t62 the full ledger, t61 the in-sample metrics, t63 and t64 the held-out ones, t7 the manifest — and the same helper functions under the same names. A reader who has read model-1 should be able to read this one without relearning anything, and should be able to diff the two scripts and see only what genuinely differs.

The proposal asks for 19 condition-specific models. It does not say which 19 items in the CCC module answer to the 19 names in Section 2.2, what to do when two of the names are the same question, how to handle a condition whose question is asked only of respondents over 35, whether the other sixteen conditions belong in the model, or which of Section 5.4’s four specifications “the same LASSO procedure” refers to. Those questions are settled here, and every settlement is recorded.

This report is built to be vetted, not merely read. As in model-1, it is organised as ten steps, each closing with a review point naming exactly what a reader should agree or disagree with before the next step is allowed to stand.

The status of these estimates

Model 2 is the definitive estimation script for Sections 5.7 and 5.8. The fitted objects, coefficient ledgers, and fold-level metrics it writes to disk are the versioned evidentiary record for those sections. Downstream reports should read those artifacts and interpret them; they should not re-estimate. Step 10 lists every artifact with the call that reloads it.

Three caveats travel with every number here and cannot be removed by re-running anything:

  1. The intervals are not the intervals the proposal asked for. Bootstrap replicate weights do not exist in the 2010 or 2014 PUMF (inherited decision 10). Three interval variants are reported instead, two of which are explicit lower bounds on the understatement.
  2. Estimation and selection used the same subgroup. The rate ratios in Step 8 are conditional on a procedure that consumed the whole subgroup. Step 9 measures how much that flatters them.
  3. A condition-specific model does not isolate its condition. It conditions on it. The subgroups overlap heavily, and Step 3 measures the overlap before any model is fitted.

Research questions:

  1. Which of the 19 chronic conditions named in Section 2.2 can actually be modelled from these two PUMF cycles, and what happens to the ones that cannot?
  2. Is each condition subgroup large enough to support a variable-selection procedure designed for a sample of fifty thousand — and by what measure of “large enough”?
  3. How far do the subgroups overlap, and what does that overlap do to the reading of a condition-specific coefficient?
  4. What does the Section 5.4 LASSO procedure retain inside each subgroup, and does the parsimonious penalty retain anything at all at this scale?
  5. Which predictors of absence are specific to a condition, and which recur across most of them?
  6. What is the adjusted prevalence rate ratio for every retained term in every subgroup, and how wide is the interval once the missing bootstrap is accounted for?
  7. How well does each condition-specific model predict on respondents it has not seen, and how stable is its selected variable list when a fifth of a small subgroup is withheld?

Definition of Terms

Condition roster. The table mapping each of the 19 constructs Section 2.2 names onto the CCC item that answers it. Two of the nineteen have no item of their own, so nineteen requested models resolve to seventeen fitted ones. Step 1 establishes this before any estimation.

Index condition. The condition whose subgroup is being modelled. It is constant inside its own subgroup by construction and therefore carries no information there, so it is removed from the candidate set — and only from that one model.

Main frame / age 35+ frame. Two complete-case frames. The main frame is model-1’s analytic sample, unchanged, and hosts sixteen subgroups. The age 35+ frame additionally requires the COPD item to be observed, which restricts it to respondents old enough to have been asked. It hosts one subgroup.

Comorbidity. The presence of conditions other than the index one. The subgroups are not disjoint: most respondents in any subgroup carry at least one other condition. The other sixteen conditions therefore remain in the candidate set, so a coefficient in Table 4 is adjusted for what else the respondent carries.

lambda.min / lambda.1se. The penalty minimising cross-validated deviance, and the largest penalty whose deviance remains within one standard error of that minimum. At the scale of a condition subgroup the second frequently returns nothing at all, which is why the first is designated primary here and the second is reported as a sensitivity.

Empty selection. A specification that retained no variable beyond the unpenalised cycle indicator. It is a legitimate result and it is counted, not hidden: Table t5 reports how often each penalty produced one.

Unstable term. A term whose standard error exceeds 2 on the log scale, meaning its rate-ratio interval spans more than four orders of magnitude. It arises when a factor level is represented by a handful of respondents in a small subgroup. Such terms are marked rather than removed; their point estimates should not be quoted.

Respondents per design column. The subgroup size divided by the number of columns offered to the penalty. Section 5.7 flags subgroups below 500 respondents; this ratio is the quantity that actually governs whether a selection procedure has anything to work with, and it is reported beside the count of respondents with at least one day absent.

Held out. Computed on respondents the model was not fitted to. Section 5.8 asks for held-out error explicitly, and it is not the same quantity as the in-sample error a single fit reports.

local_root <- "./analysis/model-2/"
local_data <- paste0(local_root, "data-local/")
fits_folder <- paste0(local_data, "fits/")
prints_folder <- paste0(local_root, "prints/")
path_parquet <- "./data-private/derived/cchs-2-tables/cchs_analytic.parquet"

outcome_var <- "days_absent_total"
weight_col <- "wts_m_pooled"
cycle_var <- "cchs_cycle_f"
forced_vars <- cycle_var
lasso_seed <- 42
lasso_folds <- 5

# The COPD item is administered only to respondents aged 35 and over, so it
# cannot sit on the primary complete-case frame (model-1 decision 2). It gets a
# supplementary frame of its own here, because Section 5.7 conditions ON the
# disease and everyone who reports COPD was asked the question by construction.
# Decision 21.
copd_var <- "cc_copd"

# Section 5.8 performance cross-validation. Named apart from `lasso_folds` for
# the same reason as in model-1: that one tunes the penalty inside glmnet on a
# Poisson deviance, this one estimates out-of-sample prediction error for the
# negative binomial refits. Both are five-fold because Sections 5.4 and 5.8 both
# say five; they are not the same folds and they answer different questions.
perf_folds <- 5
perf_seed <- 42

# Subgroup feasibility thresholds. Section 5.7 names 500 unweighted as the flag
# threshold; `min_fit_n` is the point below which a model is not attempted at
# all. Decision 26.
small_subgroup_n <- 500L
min_fit_n <- 100L

# A term whose standard error exceeds this on the log scale has an interval
# spanning more than four orders of magnitude on the rate-ratio scale. It is
# reported and marked rather than removed. Decision 27.
unstable_se <- 2

# Step 9 refits every specification on every fold twice over, for every
# condition, so the block is cached. Set TRUE to rebuild.
force_refit_cv <- FALSE
cv_cache_path <- paste0(fits_folder, "cv-performance.rds")

for (folder in c(local_data, fits_folder, prints_folder)) {
  if (!fs::dir_exists(folder)) { fs::dir_create(folder, recurse = TRUE) }
}

Helpers for subgroup construction, penalised fitting, and negative binomial refitting 
# Render a data frame as styled HTML for Quarto, or plainly for console use.
# Tall tables get a fixed-height scroll box so the report stays navigable.
print_table <- function(data, caption, align = NULL, scroll_height = NULL) {
  if (is.null(scroll_height) && nrow(data) > 25) scroll_height <- "600px"
  boxed <- data %>%
    knitr::kable(
      format = "html", caption = caption, escape = FALSE,
      align = align, row.names = FALSE
    ) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE
    )
  boxed <- if (is.null(scroll_height)) {
    kableExtra::scroll_box(boxed, width = "100%")
  } else {
    kableExtra::scroll_box(boxed, width = "100%", height = scroll_height)
  }
  cat(as.character(boxed))
  invisible(data)
}

to_yes_no <- function(x) {
  factor(ifelse(x %in% c(1, TRUE), "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes"))
}

# Strip the variable-name prefix from a design column to recover the level
# label. Vectorised, because sub() uses only the first element of `pattern`.
strip_variable_prefix <- function(column, variable) {
  purrr::map2_chr(column, variable, ~ sub(paste0("^", .y), "", .x))
}

# Does this column carry any information? A factor reduced to one level inside a
# subgroup cannot be dummy-coded, and a constant numeric contributes nothing.
is_informative <- function(x) {
  if (is.factor(x)) return(nlevels(droplevels(x)) > 1L)
  length(unique(x[!is.na(x)])) > 1L
}

# Apply the model-1 recoding contract to a selection of source columns. Factored
# out here because model-2 builds two frames rather than one (decision 21) and
# they must be recoded identically or the COPD model stops being comparable.
prepare_frame <- function(extra_vars = character(0)) {
  ds0 %>%
    select(all_of(unique(c(outcome_var, weight_col, cycle_var, lasso_vars, extra_vars)))) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.ordered), ~ factor(., ordered = FALSE))) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.logical), to_yes_no)) %>%
    mutate(across(any_of(c("dhhgle5", "dhhg611", "dhhgl12")), to_yes_no)) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.character), factor))
}

# Build a design matrix and the column-to-variable map that makes selection
# results interpretable. Reference contrasts; intercept dropped. Shared verbatim
# with model-1.
build_design <- function(model_frame, term_vars) {
  model_formula <- stats::reformulate(term_vars)
  mm <- stats::model.matrix(model_formula, data = model_frame)
  assign_index <- attr(mm, "assign")
  term_labels <- attr(stats::terms(model_formula, data = model_frame), "term.labels")
  source_variable <- c("(Intercept)", term_labels)[assign_index + 1]
  keep <- colnames(mm) != "(Intercept)"

  list(
    x = mm[, keep, drop = FALSE],
    map = tibble::tibble(
      column = colnames(mm)[keep],
      variable = source_variable[keep]
    ) %>%
      mutate(level = strip_variable_prefix(column, variable))
  )
}

# Stage 1. A weighted, L1-penalised Poisson fit with the cycle indicator exempt
# from the penalty, plus the full coefficient path for plotting. Shared verbatim
# with model-1.
fit_lasso <- function(design, outcome, weights, seed) {
  penalty_vector <- as.numeric(!design$map$variable %in% forced_vars)

  set.seed(seed)
  path <- glmnet::glmnet(
    x = design$x, y = outcome, family = "poisson", alpha = 1,
    weights = weights, penalty.factor = penalty_vector
  )
  set.seed(seed)
  cv <- suppressWarnings(glmnet::cv.glmnet(
    x = design$x, y = outcome, family = "poisson", alpha = 1,
    nfolds = lasso_folds, weights = weights, penalty.factor = penalty_vector
  ))
  list(path = path, cv = cv, penalty = penalty_vector)
}

# Extract the coefficient vector at a named lambda, joined to the column map.
coefficients_at <- function(lasso, design, lambda_rule) {
  coefficient_matrix <- stats::coef(lasso$cv, s = lambda_rule)
  tibble::tibble(
    column = rownames(coefficient_matrix),
    estimate = as.numeric(coefficient_matrix)
  ) %>%
    filter(column != "(Intercept)") %>%
    left_join(design$map, by = "column") %>%
    mutate(retained = estimate != 0)
}

# Decision 9 (inherited): a variable is promoted to stage 2 if ANY of its
# columns survived the penalty.
retained_variables <- function(coefficient_table) {
  coefficient_table %>%
    filter(retained) %>%
    pull(variable) %>%
    unique()
}

# Stage 2. Unpenalised negative binomial on the retained variable set. Wrapped
# in tryCatch because Section 5.7 anticipates non-convergence in small
# subgroups and asks for it to be reported rather than hidden.
fit_nb <- function(model_frame, term_vars, outcome) {
  usable <- term_vars[purrr::map_lgl(term_vars, ~ is_informative(model_frame[[.x]]))]
  terms_used <- if (length(usable) > 0) usable else "1"
  model_formula <- stats::reformulate(terms_used, response = outcome)
  environment(model_formula) <- environment()
  tryCatch(
    suppressWarnings(
      MASS::glm.nb(
        model_formula, data = model_frame, weights = weight_scaled,
        control = stats::glm.control(maxit = 100)
      )
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
}

# Huber-White sandwich covariance for a weighted negative binomial fit, with
# theta held at its estimate. The unequal-weighting component of the design
# effect and nothing more: strata and PSUs are suppressed in the PUMF, so the
# clustering component is not recoverable. Inherited decision 15.
# Shared verbatim with model-00 and model-1. If one changes, all must change, or
# Tables 2, 3 and 4 stop being comparable.
robust_vcov <- function(nb_fit) {
  design <- stats::model.matrix(nb_fit)
  mu <- stats::fitted(nb_fit)
  y <- nb_fit$y
  w <- nb_fit$prior.weights
  score <- w * (y - mu) / (1 + mu / nb_fit$theta)
  bread <- stats::vcov(nb_fit)
  meat <- crossprod(design * score)
  bread %*% meat %*% bread
}

# Kish's approximate design effect from unequal weighting alone. Its square root
# is the factor by which a design-based standard error would exceed the
# model-based one if weighting were the only departure from simple random
# sampling. A lower bound. Computed per subgroup here, per decision 29.
kish_design_effect <- function(w) {
  length(w) * sum(w^2) / (sum(w)^2)
}

# Wald summary on the rate-ratio scale, carrying three interval variants:
#   - Wald        model-based, understates uncertainty (inherited decision 10)
#   - robust      Huber-White sandwich, sees unequal weighting only
#   - Kish        Wald inflated by sqrt(design effect), applied uniformly
# NOT bootstrap: the replicate weights Section 5.7 assumes do not exist in the
# 2010 or 2014 PUMF. Inherited decisions 10 and 15.
tidy_nb <- function(nb_fit, column_map, deff = 1) {
  robust_se <- tryCatch(sqrt(diag(robust_vcov(nb_fit))), error = function(e) NULL)

  out <- summary(nb_fit)$coefficients %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("column") %>%
    rename(estimate = Estimate, std_error = `Std. Error`, p_value = `Pr(>|z|)`) %>%
    filter(column != "(Intercept)") %>%
    left_join(column_map, by = "column")

  out %>%
    mutate(
      se_robust = if (is.null(robust_se)) NA_real_ else unname(robust_se[column]),
      se_kish = std_error * sqrt(deff),
      p_robust = 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(estimate / se_robust)),
      rate_ratio = exp(estimate),
      ci_low = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std_error),
      ci_high = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std_error),
      ci_low_robust = exp(estimate - 1.96 * se_robust),
      ci_high_robust = exp(estimate + 1.96 * se_robust),
      ci_low_kish = exp(estimate - 1.96 * se_kish),
      ci_high_kish = exp(estimate + 1.96 * se_kish),
      unstable = std_error > unstable_se
    )
}

# Section 5.8's C-statistic, adapted to a count outcome (inherited decision 17).
# Pairs tied on the outcome carry no information about discrimination and are
# excluded from the denominator, so the comparable share travels with the
# statistic. Returns NA rather than failing when a subgroup is too thin or too
# uniform for concordance to be defined.
harrell_c <- function(observed, predicted, weights) {
  empty <- tibble::tibble(c_statistic = NA_real_, c_se = NA_real_,
                          comparable_share = NA_real_)
  if (length(unique(observed)) < 2L || length(observed) < 3L) return(empty)
  tryCatch({
    fit <- survival::concordance(observed ~ predicted, weights = weights)
    counts <- fit$count
    comparable <- sum(counts[c("concordant", "discordant", "tied.x")])
    total <- comparable + sum(counts[c("tied.y", "tied.xy")])
    tibble::tibble(
      c_statistic = as.numeric(fit$concordance),
      c_se = sqrt(as.numeric(fit$var)),
      comparable_share = comparable / total
    )
  }, error = function(e) empty)
}

# Negative binomial log-likelihood on held-out rows, using the coefficients and
# the theta estimated on the training rows. Weighted, per inherited decision 19.
nb_loglik <- function(observed, predicted, theta, weights) {
  sum(weights * stats::dnbinom(observed, size = theta, mu = predicted, log = TRUE))
}

# Deterministic fold assignment. Every condition, specification and CV variant
# scores the same partition of its own subgroup, so differences between them are
# differences in model rather than luck of the draw.
assign_folds <- function(n, k, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  sample(rep_len(seq_len(k), n))
}

# One training/testing pass for a GIVEN term set. Both CV variants of Step 9
# call this; they differ only in where `term_vars` comes from.
#
# This is model-1's `evaluate_fold()` with three subgroup guards added, because
# a fifth of a two-thousand-respondent subgroup is a much thinner object than a
# fifth of the Section 5.5 sample:
#   1. terms that go constant in the training fold are dropped and counted
#   2. test rows carrying a factor level the training fold never saw are dropped
#      and counted, rather than allowed to propagate NA through the metrics
#   3. a fold whose fit fails returns a row marked `converged = FALSE` rather
#      than aborting the condition, as Section 5.7 requires
evaluate_fold <- function(frame, train_rows, test_rows, term_vars, outcome) {
  failed <- tibble::tibble(
    n_train = length(train_rows), n_test = length(test_rows), n_unscorable = NA_integer_,
    n_terms = NA_integer_, theta = NA_real_, converged = FALSE,
    rmse = NA_real_, mae = NA_real_, loglik = NA_real_, mcfadden_r2 = NA_real_,
    c_statistic = NA_real_, c_se = NA_real_, comparable_share = NA_real_
  )

  train <- droplevels(frame[train_rows, , drop = FALSE])
  test <- frame[test_rows, , drop = FALSE]

  term_vars <- term_vars[purrr::map_lgl(term_vars, ~ is_informative(train[[.x]]))]

  factor_terms <- term_vars[purrr::map_lgl(term_vars, ~ is.factor(train[[.x]]))]
  scorable <- rep(TRUE, nrow(test))
  for (this_var in factor_terms) {
    scorable <- scorable & as.character(test[[this_var]]) %in% levels(train[[this_var]])
  }
  n_dropped <- sum(!scorable)
  test <- test[scorable, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(test) < 3L) return(failed)
  for (this_var in factor_terms) {
    test[[this_var]] <- factor(as.character(test[[this_var]]),
                               levels = levels(train[[this_var]]))
  }

  fit <- fit_nb(train, term_vars, outcome)
  fit_null <- fit_nb(train, character(0), outcome)
  if (is.null(fit) || is.null(fit_null)) return(failed)

  predicted <- tryCatch(stats::predict(fit, newdata = test, type = "response"),
                        error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(predicted) || anyNA(predicted)) return(failed)
  predicted_null <- stats::predict(fit_null, newdata = test, type = "response")
  observed <- test[[outcome]]
  w <- test$weight_scaled

  loglik_test <- nb_loglik(observed, predicted, fit$theta, w)
  loglik_test_null <- nb_loglik(observed, predicted_null, fit_null$theta, w)

  dplyr::bind_cols(
    tibble::tibble(
      n_train = nrow(train),
      n_test = nrow(test),
      n_unscorable = n_dropped,
      n_terms = length(stats::coef(fit)) - 1L,
      theta = fit$theta,
      converged = isTRUE(fit$converged),
      rmse = sqrt(stats::weighted.mean((observed - predicted)^2, w)),
      mae = stats::weighted.mean(abs(observed - predicted), w),
      loglik = loglik_test,
      mcfadden_r2 = 1 - loglik_test / loglik_test_null
    ),
    harrell_c(observed, predicted, w)
  )
}

# Cut a condition subgroup out of its frame and re-scale its weights to mean 1
# (decision 30). Unused factor levels are dropped here, once, so that every
# downstream step sees the same subgroup.
build_subgroup <- function(frame, condition_var) {
  frame %>%
    filter(.data[[condition_var]] == "Yes") %>%
    droplevels() %>%
    mutate(weight_scaled = .data[[weight_col]] / mean(.data[[weight_col]]))
}

# The candidate set offered to the penalty inside one subgroup (decisions 23
# and 24): the primary Section 5.5 predictor set, minus the index condition,
# minus anything that has gone constant. The other sixteen conditions stay.
subgroup_candidates <- function(subgroup, condition_var, candidates) {
  offered <- setdiff(candidates, condition_var)
  offered[purrr::map_lgl(offered, ~ is_informative(subgroup[[.x]]))]
}

# The whole stage-one pipeline for one condition, from frame to cross-validated
# penalised fit. Returns everything the later steps need, including what it had
# to drop, so that Table t2 can report the cost of the subgroup restriction.
fit_condition <- function(condition_var) {
  frame_id <- fitted_conditions$frame[fitted_conditions$variable == condition_var]
  subgroup <- build_subgroup(frames[[frame_id]], condition_var)

  offered <- subgroup_candidates(subgroup, condition_var, vars_excluding_perceived)
  dropped <- setdiff(setdiff(vars_excluding_perceived, condition_var), offered)
  forced_here <- forced_vars[purrr::map_lgl(forced_vars, ~ is_informative(subgroup[[.x]]))]

  feasible <- nrow(subgroup) >= min_fit_n && length(offered) > 0
  design <- if (feasible) build_design(subgroup, c(forced_here, offered)) else NULL
  lasso <- if (feasible) {
    tryCatch(
      fit_lasso(design, subgroup[[outcome_var]], subgroup$weight_scaled, lasso_seed),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
  } else {
    NULL
  }

  list(
    condition = condition_var,
    frame_id = frame_id,
    subgroup = subgroup,
    offered = offered,
    dropped = dropped,
    forced = forced_here,
    design = design,
    lasso = lasso,
    kish_deff = kish_design_effect(subgroup[[weight_col]])
  )
}

# Two frames, recoded identically (decisions 21 and 22).

#         one of them is a strict subset of the Section 5.5 analytic sample.

#         is administered only from age 35, requiring it is what restricts the
#         frame; no explicit age filter is applied or needed. This frame exists
#         only to host the COPD subgroup.
ds_model_raw <- prepare_frame()

n_source <- nrow(ds_model_raw)
complete_flag <- stats::complete.cases(ds_model_raw)

ds1 <- ds_model_raw %>%
  filter(complete_flag) %>%
  mutate(.respondent_id = dplyr::row_number())

ds_copd_raw <- prepare_frame(copd_var)

  filter(stats::complete.cases(.)) %>%
  mutate(.respondent_id = dplyr::row_number())

frames <- list(main = ds1, age35 = ds2)

n_analytic <- nrow(ds1)
n_analytic_copd <- nrow(ds2)

)

  stats::setNames("Survey design", cycle_var)
)
condition_labels <- stats::setNames(
  variable_labels[fitted_conditions$variable], fitted_conditions$variable
)

                          Stroke   187           2.735          37.99      13.89     57.8%  34

Equidispersion would put variance / mean at 1. No subgroup is close, so
stage two is negative binomial in every one of them, exactly as in model-1.
Note also that the zero share stays high inside every subgroup: conditioning
on a chronic condition does not turn this into a dense count outcome.
Reading the subgroup outcome summary

Two features govern everything downstream. The variance-to-mean ratio stays far above 1 in every subgroup, so stage two is negative binomial throughout, exactly as in model-1. And the share of respondents at zero days stays high even after conditioning on a chronic condition — selecting on disease raises the mean but does not make this a dense count. That second fact is why the C-statistic in Step 9 is a narrow instrument here, and why RMSE moves in directions that likelihood-based measures do not.

Analysis

Step 1 — The Condition Roster

Section 5.7 says “each of the 19 chronic conditions.” Establishing what those nineteen are, in terms of items that exist in the 2010 and 2014 Public Use Microdata Files, is the first substantive act of the report — and it does not come out to nineteen.

Table t11 carries both sample sizes Section 5.7 asks for — unweighted \(n\) and weighted \(N\) — and one it does not: the number of respondents in each subgroup reporting at least one day absent. That third column is the one to read. A negative binomial model of a count outcome learns from variation in the count, and a subgroup of a thousand respondents of whom two hundred have a non-zero outcome is a thinner object than its \(n\) suggests.

Review point 1

Agree or disagree with the mapping in Table t1. Three specific questions:

  1. Is collapsing “mental illness” and “mood disorder” into the single CCC item correct, or was a separate construct intended that would require a different data source?
  2. Section 2.2 pairs “cardiovascular disease/stroke” as one construct. The CCC module carries heart disease and stroke as separate items and they are modelled separately here. Should they instead be combined into one subgroup?
  3. Is “digestive diseases” genuinely absent, or is it meant to denote the bowel-disorder item under another name?

Step 2 — Subgroup Feasibility

Section 5.7 anticipates that some subgroups will be small and asks for them to be flagged at \(n < 500\). That threshold is necessary but not sufficient, because what a selection procedure needs is not respondents but respondents per parameter.

Compute per-subgroup candidate counts, design width, and verdicts 
feasibility <- purrr::map_dfr(fitted_conditions$variable, function(this_condition) {
  frame_id <- fitted_conditions$frame[fitted_conditions$variable == this_condition]
  sub <- build_subgroup(frames[[frame_id]], this_condition)
  offered <- subgroup_candidates(sub, this_condition, vars_excluding_perceived)
  dropped <- setdiff(setdiff(vars_excluding_perceived, this_condition), offered)
  forced_here <- forced_vars[purrr::map_lgl(forced_vars, ~ is_informative(sub[[.x]]))]
  n_columns <- if (length(offered) > 0) {
    ncol(build_design(sub, c(forced_here, offered))$x)
  } else {
    0L
  }
  tibble::tibble(
    condition = this_condition,
    n = nrow(sub),
    n_nonzero = sum(sub[[outcome_var]] > 0),
    n_offered = length(offered),
    n_dropped = length(dropped),
    dropped_vars = paste(variable_labels[dropped], collapse = "; "),
    n_columns = n_columns
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(
    condition_label = variable_labels[condition],
    per_column = n / pmax(n_columns, 1L),
    nonzero_per_column = n_nonzero / pmax(n_columns, 1L),
    verdict = dplyr::case_when(
      n < min_fit_n ~ "not fitted",
      n < small_subgroup_n ~ "fitted, flagged small",
      TRUE ~ "fitted"
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

readr::write_csv(feasibility, paste0(local_data, "subgroup-feasibility.csv"))

The two point series in Graph g1 are the story of this report. The filled points are the subgroup sizes Section 5.7 asks about; the hollow points are the respondents who actually contribute variation to a count model. The gap between them is roughly constant in proportion and large in every subgroup.

The final column is the honest measure. Where it falls below one, the design matrix has more columns than the subgroup has informative respondents, and the only reason estimation is possible at all is the penalty. Those rows are not invalid, but the model they produce is a description of the penalty as much as of the data, and Step 9 will show how unstable it is.

Review point 2

Agree or disagree with two thresholds and one frame.

  1. min_fit_n = 100 is the point below which no model is attempted. Section 5.7 does not name such a threshold; it asks for a flag at 500 and for non-convergence to be reported. Should the floor be higher, lower, or removed in favour of fitting everything and reporting the wreckage?

The COPD subgroup is therefore drawn from a different denominator than the other sixteen, and its age composition is restricted by construction. Is that the right trade, or should COPD be reported as unavailable?

The sum of the sixteen main-frame subgroup sizes exceeds the number of distinct respondents who have any condition, by a wide margin. That arithmetic is not a defect; it is the design of Section 5.7. But it has a consequence for interpretation that has to be settled before any coefficient is read.

A Section 5.7 model does not isolate its index condition. It selects on it. Everyone in the arthritis subgroup carries whatever else they carry, and Table t21 shows that most of them carry a good deal. This is why the other sixteen conditions stay in the candidate set (decision 24): a model of absence among people with arthritis that ignored whether they also have a mood disorder would credit arthritis with an association belonging to the pair.

It is also why “the arthritis model” is a phrase to use carefully. What Table 4 reports for that row is the predictors of absence among workers who have arthritis, adjusted for their other conditions — not the effect of arthritis, which is a Section 5.3 and 5.5 quantity and lives in model-00 and model-1.

Review point 3

Agree or disagree that the other conditions belong in each subgroup’s candidate set. The alternative — dropping them — would make each model a description of the demographic and occupational predictors within a disease group, which is arguably closer to what “predictors of absenteeism within that subgroup” means in plain reading. Decision 24 records the alternative and how to take it.

Step 4 — The Decision Registry

Model 2 inherits nineteen decisions from model-1 and makes eleven of its own. The inherited ones are listed by title only; restating their reasoning here would create a second copy that drifts from the first.

Table t1 maps every requested construct to the item that answers it, so the shortfall is visible rather than silent. condition_roster in declare-globals

Section 5.7 conditions ON the disease, so the age restriction is a property of the subgroup rather than a loss: every respondent who reports COPD was asked the question by construction. The frame is reported separately because its denominator differs from the other sixteen. Within it the ‘25-54’ age band contains only respondents aged 35-54. copd_var and frames in tweak-data-0
22 Subgroup base sample Re-derive complete cases inside each condition subgroup; filter the model-1 complete-case frame Filter the model-1 frame Re-deriving would give each condition its own denominator and its own candidate set, so no two condition models would be comparable with each other and none would be comparable with Table 3. Filtering keeps every subgroup a strict subset of the Section 5.5 analytic sample. ds1 in tweak-data-0
23 Candidate set inside a subgroup All 48 LASSO candidates; the 45 excluding perceived health; a reduced set scaled to subgroup size 45 excluding perceived health, minus the index condition, minus anything constant in the subgroup The index condition is constant inside its own subgroup and carries no information there. The perceived-health toggle belongs to the four-way comparison of Section 5.4; Section 5.7 asks for one model per condition, and the primary specification of Section 5.5 is the one that excludes perceived health. A variable that loses all but one level inside a subgroup cannot be dummy-coded and is dropped, with every drop recorded in Table t2. subgroup_candidates() in declare-functions
24 Comorbidity Drop the other 16 conditions from the candidate set; retain them Retain them Chronic conditions co-occur heavily; Table t21 quantifies how heavily. A model of absenteeism among respondents with arthritis that ignored whether they also have a mood disorder would attribute to arthritis an association belonging to the pair. The subgroups are not disjoint and these estimates are conditional, not causal, which is exactly why t21 sits upstream of the models. subgroup_candidates() in declare-functions
25 Penalty rule designated primary for subgroups lambda.1se, matching the primary model of Section 5.5; lambda.min; both Both reported; lambda.min designated primary These subgroups are one to two orders of magnitude smaller than the Section 5.5 sample. model-0 showed lambda.1se retaining nothing at all at n = 63,843 on a single domain; at subgroup scale an empty selection is the expected outcome, and a specification that names no predictors cannot answer ‘the main predictors of absenteeism within that subgroup’. Table t5 reports how often each rule returned an empty set, so the choice is checkable rather than asserted. primary_spec and condition_specs in declare-globals
26 Small-subgroup threshold No flag; the proposal’s n < 500; a rule based on the number of non-zero outcomes Flag n < 500 as Section 5.7 directs, and report non-zero respondents beside it Section 5.7 names 500 unweighted. That count is not the binding constraint for a count model: what limits estimation is the number of respondents with at least one day absent, which is well under a third of any subgroup. Both are reported. A subgroup that clears 500 but carries ninety informative respondents should be read as small. small_subgroup_n and min_fit_n in declare-globals
27 Rare levels and unstable terms Collapse rare levels; drop variables that have a rare level; retain and flag Retain and flag Collapsing changes what a coefficient means, and would have to be done differently in each subgroup, which breaks comparability. Dropping would remove province and occupation from every small subgroup. Instead, a term whose standard error exceeds 2 on the log scale is marked unstable in Table t62: its interval is uninformative and its point estimate should not be quoted. unstable_se in declare-globals
28 Section 5.8 resampling method 5-fold cross-validation; leave-one-out for small subgroups; a mixture by subgroup size 5-fold for every subgroup Section 5.8 permits leave-one-out at the analyst’s discretion. It is declined for a technical reason rather than a convenience one: Harrell’s C is computed over PAIRS of held-out respondents, and a leave-one-out fold contains a single respondent, so the C-statistic Section 5.8 requests would be undefined and the between-fold spread that makes a cross-validated number readable would not exist. Five folds also keep model-2 on the same footing as model-1’s Tables t63 and t64. Folds that fail to converge are counted, not silently dropped. perf_folds in declare-globals
29 Design effect basis Reuse model-1’s full-sample Kish design effect; compute one within each subgroup Within each subgroup A design effect describes the weight distribution of the sample whose intervals it widens. Weights inside a condition subgroup are not distributed as they are in the pooled sample, and Output out5 shows the realised value varying across conditions. Using a single number for all seventeen would understate some intervals and overstate others. build_subgroup() in declare-functions
30 Weight rescaling Carry model-1’s rescaled weight into the subgroup; rescale to mean 1 within each subgroup Rescale within each subgroup glm.nb treats prior weights as frequencies when estimating dispersion, so a subgroup whose carried-forward weights average far from 1 would return a theta on a different scale from its neighbours. Rescaling inside the subgroup makes theta comparable across conditions. Point estimates are unaffected; only the scale of the weights changes. build_subgroup() in declare-functions

The same decision cannot be reversed here either

Inherited decision 10 records that bootstrap variance estimation is impossible with these data. Section 5.7 asks for bootstrap intervals in the same words Sections 5.3, 5.5 and 5.9 use, and the answer is the same: CCHS bootstrap replicate weights begin with the 2015 cycle, neither the 2010 nor the 2014 PUMF carries them, and strata and PSU identifiers are suppressed.

Model 2 responds as model-00 and model-1 do — a Wald interval beside a Huber–White sandwich interval and a Kish-inflated interval — with one difference. The design effect is computed within each subgroup (decision 29), because the weight distribution inside a condition subgroup is not the weight distribution of the pooled sample. Output out5 shows how much it varies.

Review point 4

Read decisions 20 through 30. Decisions 20, 21 and 25 are the consequential ones: what counts as a condition, whether COPD is modelled at all, and which penalty rule is designated primary at subgroup scale. Any of them can be overturned; the “reversal” column says what to change.

Step 5 — The Two Specifications

Section 5.7 says variable selection “should follow the same LASSO procedure described in Section 5.4.” Section 5.4 describes four specifications, arranged on two axes: a perceived-health toggle and a penalty rule. Only one of those axes survives the reference.

The perceived-health toggle exists to answer a Section 5.4 question — whether self-rated health absorbs the signal carried by the individual conditions. Section 5.7 asks for one model per condition, and Section 5.5 designates the specification that excludes perceived health as primary. So model-2 carries that predictor set and reads it at both penalties, which means one cross-validated fit per condition yields both rows.

Table t4: The two specifications carried into every condition subgroup. As in model-1, one cross-validated fit per condition yields both rows: the predictor set defines the fit, the penalty selects a model from it. The perceived-health toggle is not carried, because it belongs to the four-way comparison of Section 5.4 and Section 5.7 asks for one model per condition (decision 23). lambda.min is designated primary at subgroup scale (decision 25).
Specification Role Penalty Perceived health Candidates offered Corresponds to
Permissive (min) Primary lambda.min excluded up to 44 (index condition removed) Section 5.5 Model 3
Parsimonious (1SE) Sensitivity lambda.1se excluded up to 44 (index condition removed) Section 5.5 Model 1
Review point 5

Agree or disagree that lambda.min should be designated primary inside subgroups, reversing model-1’s ordering. The argument is in decision 25 and the evidence is in Table t5: if the parsimonious rule returns an empty set in most subgroups, it cannot answer the question Section 5.7 asks, however defensible it is at full sample size. If you disagree, both specifications are estimated and reported side by side throughout, so nothing needs re-running — only the designation changes.

Step 6 — Stage One, Per-Condition Penalised Poisson

Seventeen weighted L1-penalised Poisson fits, one per subgroup, each with its own five-fold cross-validated penalty path and its own candidate set.

Fit and persist one cross-validated penalised Poisson model per condition 
condition_fits <- purrr::map(
  stats::setNames(fitted_conditions$variable, fitted_conditions$variable),
  fit_condition
)

for (this_condition in names(condition_fits)) {
  cf <- condition_fits[[this_condition]]
  if (!is.null(cf$lasso)) {
    saveRDS(cf$lasso$cv, paste0(fits_folder, "cv_", this_condition, ".rds"))
    saveRDS(cf$design$map, paste0(fits_folder, "map_", this_condition, ".rds"))
  }
}

fitted_ok <- names(condition_fits)[
  purrr::map_lgl(condition_fits, ~ !is.null(.x$lasso))
]

# Order every downstream facet and axis by subgroup size, largest first, so that
# a reader always knows roughly how much evidence sits behind a panel.
condition_order <- condition_inventory$condition[condition_inventory$condition %in% fitted_ok]
condition_factor_levels <- unname(variable_labels[condition_order])

cv_curve_data <- purrr::map_dfr(fitted_ok, function(this_condition) {
  cv <- condition_fits[[this_condition]]$lasso$cv
  tibble::tibble(
    condition = this_condition,
    lambda = cv$lambda,
    cv_mean = cv$cvm,
    cv_low = cv$cvlo,
    cv_high = cv$cvup,
    n_nonzero = cv$nzero
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(condition_label = factor(variable_labels[condition],
                                  levels = condition_factor_levels))

lambda_marks <- purrr::map_dfr(fitted_ok, function(this_condition) {
  cv <- condition_fits[[this_condition]]$lasso$cv
  tibble::tibble(
    condition = this_condition,
    lambda_rule = c("lambda.1se", "lambda.min"),
    lambda = c(cv$lambda.1se, cv$lambda.min)
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(condition_label = factor(variable_labels[condition],
                                  levels = condition_factor_levels))

path_data <- purrr::map_dfr(fitted_ok, function(this_condition) {
  cf <- condition_fits[[this_condition]]
  as.matrix(cf$lasso$path$beta) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("column") %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-column, names_to = "step", values_to = "estimate") %>%
    mutate(
      lambda = cf$lasso$path$lambda[as.integer(sub("^s", "", step)) + 1],
      condition = this_condition
    ) %>%
    left_join(cf$design$map, by = "column")
}) %>%
  mutate(
    domain = variable_domains[variable],
    condition_label = factor(variable_labels[condition],
                             levels = condition_factor_levels)
  )

Panels are ordered by subgroup size, so the sequence of small multiples is also a sequence in statistical power. The quantity to read across them is the width of the one-standard-error band relative to the depth of the minimum. Where the band is wide and the curve shallow, cross-validation cannot distinguish penalties over a broad range, and lambda.1se will sit far to the right of lambda.min and discard nearly everything.

Reading each panel right to left, the order in which coefficients leave zero is the order in which that subgroup insists on them. Comparing panels shows whether the same domains lead in every condition or whether each disease has its own hierarchy.

Review point 6

Agree or disagree with the fitting choices, which are inherited unchanged from model-1: five folds, seed 42, survey weights passed to cv.glmnet, cycle exempt from the penalty. The one new consideration is that five folds of a subgroup are much thinner than five folds of the Section 5.5 sample, which is visible in the width of the bands in Graph g2.

Graph g4 is this report’s central artifact, and it is read in two directions.

Reading down a column gives one condition’s whole verdict: the variables that predict absence among workers who have that disease. That is the Section 5.7 deliverable in visual form.

Reading across a row gives something Section 5.7 does not ask for but which falls out of asking it seventeen times. A variable coloured across many columns predicts absence more or less regardless of which chronic condition a worker carries; a variable coloured in one or two columns is specific to those diseases. The first kind belongs in a general model of absence, which is what model-1 estimates. The second kind is what a condition-specific analysis exists to find.

Review point 7

This is the report’s substantive output alongside Table 4. Two questions to settle:

  1. Are the recurring rows in Graph g4 genuine cross-condition predictors, or are they variables that a large subgroup can afford to retain and a small one cannot? The subgroup-size ordering of the columns is there to make that check possible; a row that fills the left of the grid and empties toward the right is a power artifact, not a finding.
  2. Should “retained” continue to mean “at least one design column survived”? Inherited decision 9 records the alternative. It matters more here than in model-1, because a factor with many levels retained on the strength of one thin cell contributes a term that Table t62 may then mark unstable.

Step 8 — Stage Two, Negative Binomial Estimation

Each retained set is re-estimated without penalty under a negative binomial likelihood, inside its own subgroup. This step answers Section 5.7 and produces deliverable Table 4. Before the estimates, the instruments used to bracket their uncertainty.

Fit and persist the condition-specific negative binomial models 
nb_keys <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  condition = fitted_ok,
  spec_id = condition_specs$spec_id
) %>%
  mutate(key = paste0(condition, "__", spec_id))

spec_terms <- purrr::set_names(
  purrr::map2(nb_keys$condition, nb_keys$spec_id, function(this_condition, this_spec) {
    kept <- selection_long %>%
      filter(condition == this_condition, spec_id == this_spec) %>%
      retained_variables()
    union(condition_fits[[this_condition]]$forced,
          setdiff(kept, condition_fits[[this_condition]]$forced))
  }),
  nb_keys$key
)

nb_fits <- purrr::imap(spec_terms, function(term_vars, this_key) {
  this_condition <- sub("__.*$", "", this_key)
  fit_nb(condition_fits[[this_condition]]$subgroup, term_vars, outcome_var)
})

nb_nulls <- purrr::map(
  stats::setNames(fitted_ok, fitted_ok),
  ~ fit_nb(condition_fits[[.x]]$subgroup, character(0), outcome_var)
)

for (this_key in names(nb_fits)) {
  if (!is.null(nb_fits[[this_key]])) {
    saveRDS(nb_fits[[this_key]], paste0(fits_folder, "nb_", this_key, ".rds"))
  }
}
saveRDS(nb_nulls, paste0(fits_folder, "nb_nulls.rds"))

nb_coefficients <- purrr::imap_dfr(nb_fits, function(fit, this_key) {
  if (is.null(fit)) return(tibble::tibble())
  this_condition <- sub("__.*$", "", this_key)
  this_spec <- sub("^.*__", "", this_key)
  tidy_nb(fit, condition_fits[[this_condition]]$design$map,
          deff = condition_fits[[this_condition]]$kish_deff) %>%
    mutate(condition = this_condition, spec_id = this_spec)
}) %>%
  left_join(condition_specs %>% select(spec_id, model_label, role), by = "spec_id") %>%
  mutate(
    domain = variable_domains[variable],
    variable_label = variable_labels[variable],
    condition_label = variable_labels[condition],
    term = paste0(variable_label, ifelse(level == "", "", paste0(": ", level)))
  )

readr::write_csv(nb_coefficients, paste0(local_data, "nb-coefficients.csv"))
Output out5: Variance-estimation instruments for Section 5.7
Section 5.7 asks for 500 bootstrap replicate weights, the same instrument
Sections 5.3 and 5.5 ask for. They do not exist in the 2010 or 2014 PUMF
(inherited decision 10), and strata and PSU identifiers are suppressed, so
no fully design-based variance estimator can be built for any subgroup.
What follows are two LOWER bounds on how far the model-based intervals
understate uncertainty. Neither sees clustering.

Huber-White sandwich SE multiplier, over every term in every fitted model:
  median: 1.321
  range:  0.000 to 3.434
  terms:  572
The spread is wider than model-1's because subgroup cells are thinner. A
multiplier below 1 is not a narrowing of the true interval; it is a thin
cell in which the sandwich estimator is itself unreliable. Table t62
reports all three interval variants side by side and marks terms whose
standard error exceeds 2 on the log scale (decision 27).

The design effect varies across subgroups, which is the reason it is computed within them rather than inherited from the pooled sample. A single number applied to all seventeen would widen some intervals too much and others not enough, and the direction of the error would be unknowable from the table.

The sandwich multipliers spread more widely than they do in model-1, and the low end of that spread should not be read as good news. A multiplier below 1 means the sandwich estimator has landed in a cell too thin to estimate its own variance reliably; it is a symptom of the same smallness that decision 27 flags, not a demonstration that the model-based interval was conservative.

A blank cell means the term was not retained under that penalty. These are NOT bootstrap intervals (inherited decision 10), and they ignore the selection step that produced the term list. Table t62 carries the log-scale coefficients, standard errors, exact p-values and two wider interval variants.

Table t62 is the compliance artifact: every quantity Section 5.7 names — unweighted \(n\), weighted \(N\), coefficient, prevalence rate ratio, interval and Wald \(p\)-value — for every term in every condition-specific model. Read the three interval columns together, as in model-1: where the Wald and Kish intervals agree about whether they contain 1, the conclusion survives the weighting problem; where they disagree, the term is unresolved rather than null or significant.

Read the UNSTABLE flag first, though. A term carrying it comes from a factor level held up by a handful of respondents, and its interval is uninformative regardless of what the three variants say about it.

Graph g5 takes the terms retained in the greatest number of subgroups and shows their estimates wherever they were retained, with conditions ordered by subgroup size. A term whose rate ratios cluster tightly across many diseases is a general predictor of absence that happens to have been found seventeen times over. A term whose rate ratios scatter is either genuinely condition-dependent or under-determined, and the ordering by subgroup size usually tells which.

One warning about Table t61 that does not apply to model-1’s version of it: these rows are not comparable across conditions. Each is computed on a different subgroup, of a different size, with a different outcome distribution. AIC and BIC in particular are computed from a weighted pseudo-likelihood on different data, so a smaller AIC in one row says nothing whatever about the row above it. Read the table down a condition — comparing the two specifications within a disease — and never across.

Output out3 answers Section 5.7’s explicit request that non-convergence be reported. It also counts the empty selections, which are not failures but are results a reader needs to see stated rather than inferred from a blank row in Table 4.

Review point 8

Agree or disagree that Tables t6 and t62 are fit to serve as the study’s Table 4. The specific questions to settle:

  1. Should conditions flagged small in Table t11 be published at all, or reported as attempted-and-withheld? Section 5.7 asks for a flag, which is what is implemented; a stricter reading would suppress them.
  2. Is the UNSTABLE flag at a standard error of 2 on the log scale the right threshold, and should flagged terms be shown or withheld?
  3. Should the deliverable table carry both penalty rules, or should one be chosen and the other relegated to an appendix?

Step 9 — Section 5.8, Held-Out Performance

Section 5.8 asks for AIC, BIC, McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\), a C-statistic, and RMSE and MAE “computed on the withheld test fold,” averaged over five folds, for every condition-specific model. Table t61 gave the in-sample versions. This step supplies the rest.

It also declines an invitation. Section 5.8 offers leave-one-out as an option for small subgroups, at the analyst’s discretion. It is declined for a technical reason rather than a convenience one: Harrell’s C is computed over pairs of held-out respondents, and a leave-one-out fold contains one respondent. The C-statistic Section 5.8 asks for in the same paragraph would be undefined, and the between-fold spread that makes a cross-validated number readable would not exist. Five folds also keep model-2 on the same footing as model-1’s Tables t63 and t64. Decision 28.

Five-fold cross-validation of every condition and specification, both variants 
if (!force_refit_cv && file.exists(cv_cache_path)) {
  cv_performance <- readRDS(cv_cache_path)
  cat("Loaded cached cross-validation results from ", cv_cache_path, "\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("Refitting the Section 5.8 cross-validation. This is the slow block.\n")
  cv_start_time <- Sys.time()

  cv_performance <- purrr::map_dfr(fitted_ok, function(this_condition) {
    cf <- condition_fits[[this_condition]]
    sub <- cf$subgroup
    fold_id <- assign_folds(nrow(sub), perf_folds, perf_seed)
    cat("  ", this_condition, " (n = ", nrow(sub), ")\n", sep = "")

    purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(perf_folds), function(this_fold) {
      test_rows <- which(fold_id == this_fold)
      train_rows <- which(fold_id != this_fold)

      # Variant A - term set fixed at what the full subgroup selected.
      fixed <- purrr::pmap_dfr(
        condition_specs %>% select(spec_id),
        function(spec_id) {
          term_vars <- spec_terms[[paste0(this_condition, "__", spec_id)]]
          evaluate_fold(sub, train_rows, test_rows, term_vars, outcome_var) %>%
            mutate(condition = this_condition, spec_id = spec_id,
                   fold = this_fold, variant = "fixed term set")
        }
      )

      # Variant B - the whole two-stage procedure re-run inside the training
      # fold, so no held-out respondent contributed to selection.
      train_frame <- droplevels(sub[train_rows, , drop = FALSE])
      fold_offered <- subgroup_candidates(train_frame, this_condition,
                                          vars_excluding_perceived)
      fold_forced <- forced_vars[
        purrr::map_lgl(forced_vars, ~ is_informative(train_frame[[.x]]))
      ]
      fold_design <- if (length(fold_offered) > 0) {
        build_design(train_frame, c(fold_forced, fold_offered))
      } else {
        NULL
      }
      fold_lasso <- if (!is.null(fold_design)) {
        tryCatch(
          fit_lasso(fold_design, train_frame[[outcome_var]],
                    train_frame$weight_scaled, lasso_seed),
          error = function(e) NULL
        )
      } else {
        NULL
      }

      reselected <- purrr::pmap_dfr(
        condition_specs %>% select(spec_id, lambda_rule),
        function(spec_id, lambda_rule) {
          term_vars <- if (is.null(fold_lasso)) {
            fold_forced
          } else {
            kept <- coefficients_at(fold_lasso, fold_design, lambda_rule) %>%
              retained_variables()
            union(fold_forced, setdiff(kept, fold_forced))
          }
          evaluate_fold(sub, train_rows, test_rows, term_vars, outcome_var) %>%
            mutate(condition = this_condition, spec_id = spec_id,
                   fold = this_fold, variant = "selection re-run",
                   n_vars_selected = length(term_vars))
        }
      )

      bind_rows(fixed, reselected)
    })
  }) %>%
    left_join(condition_specs %>% select(spec_id, model_label, role), by = "spec_id") %>%
    mutate(condition_label = variable_labels[condition])

  attr(cv_performance, "elapsed_minutes") <-
    as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), cv_start_time, units = "mins"))
  saveRDS(cv_performance, cv_cache_path)
}

readr::write_csv(cv_performance, paste0(local_data, "cv-performance-folds.csv"))

cv_summary <- cv_performance %>%
  group_by(variant, condition, condition_label, spec_id, model_label) %>%
  summarise(
    folds_converged = sum(converged),
    n_terms_mean = mean(n_terms, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_terms_range = if (all(is.na(n_terms))) {
      "n/a"
    } else {
      paste0(min(n_terms, na.rm = TRUE), "-", max(n_terms, na.rm = TRUE))
    },
    rmse_mean = mean(rmse, na.rm = TRUE), rmse_sd = stats::sd(rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
    mae_mean = mean(mae, na.rm = TRUE), mae_sd = stats::sd(mae, na.rm = TRUE),
    mcfadden_mean = mean(mcfadden_r2, na.rm = TRUE),
    mcfadden_sd = stats::sd(mcfadden_r2, na.rm = TRUE),
    c_mean = mean(c_statistic, na.rm = TRUE), c_sd = stats::sd(c_statistic, na.rm = TRUE),
    comparable_share = mean(comparable_share, na.rm = TRUE),
    unscorable = sum(n_unscorable, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(condition_inventory %>% select(condition, n), by = "condition") %>%
  arrange(variant, desc(n), spec_id)

readr::write_csv(cv_summary, paste0(local_data, "cv-performance-summary.csv"))

Table t63 is the literal answer to Section 5.8: the term set is what the full subgroup’s LASSO chose, and the negative binomial is refitted five times with a fifth of the subgroup withheld each time. It is also, for that reason, optimistic — the penalty that produced the term list saw every respondent it is now being scored on.

In subgroups this size that range is the honest description of what Section 5.7 can and cannot establish.

Table t64 removes that advantage by re-running the whole two-stage procedure inside each training fold. The term-count range is the column to read first. Model 1 found the selected set unstable even at forty-nine thousand respondents, ranging from eight to thirty-eight terms across folds. At subgroup scale the same measurement is the honest description of what a condition-specific selection can and cannot establish.

Graph g6 shows the five folds individually rather than only their mean, for the primary specification. Where the fold points for a condition scatter across the panel, the mean printed in Table t63 is not a number to quote, and the spread — not the mean — is the result.

A positive d McFadden or d C is the amount by which evaluating a model on
data that helped select it flatters that model. model-1 found this quantity

orders of magnitude, so the same reassurance should not be assumed here;
the table above is where it is either earned or lost.

The C-statistic is narrower here than in model-1

Harrell’s C counts only pairs of respondents who differ on the outcome. Conditioning on a chronic condition raises mean days absent but leaves most respondents at zero, so most pairs remain incomparable and never enter the denominator. The comparable share is reported beside every C in Table t63 for that reason. A C of 0.63 computed on a third of pairs in a subgroup of eight hundred is a much weaker claim than the same number computed on half of pairs in a sample of forty-nine thousand, and the two should not be set side by side without that qualification.

Review point 9

Three questions.

  1. Which table is the Section 5.8 deliverable — t63, which follows the proposal’s wording, or t64, which is what the numbers would be on new data? Model 1 found the gap negligible; whether that holds at subgroup scale is exactly what out6 measures, and the answer should decide this.
  2. Does the term-count range in t64 change how a condition-specific variable list may be described in the manuscript? For most subgroups the honest sentence is likely to be about the estimates rather than about the identity of the selected set.
  3. Is five-fold cross-validation defensible for the smallest subgroups, or should those rows be reported without cross-validated metrics at all rather than with metrics whose between-fold spread swamps their mean?

Step 10 — Reproducibility Ledger

Every fitted object and every intermediate table is written to disk, so a reviewer can re-open any result without re-running the estimation, and so that downstream reports can cite these artifacts as fixed rather than recompute them.

What Model 2 Settles, and What It Does Not

Settled.

  • The nineteen conditions Section 2.2 names are mapped onto the items the PUMF carries, and the shortfall to seventeen is documented rather than silently absorbed.
  • COPD, which model-1 had to exclude, is recovered on a frame where its question was actually asked.
  • Section 5.7. A condition-specific model is estimated for every analysable condition, under both penalty rules, with both sample sizes reported and small subgroups flagged as the section directs.
  • Deliverable Table 4 is produced in two forms: a rate-ratio grid (t6) and a full ledger carrying log coefficients, standard errors, exact \(p\)-values and three interval variants (t62).
  • Section 5.8. All five requested metrics are reported, in-sample (t61) and on withheld folds (t63), with an honest-selection counterpart (t64) that quantifies how much of the apparent performance is optimism and how far the selected set moves under refitting.
  • Non-convergence and empty selections are counted and named, as Section 5.7 requires.
  • The overlap between subgroups is measured before any model is fitted, so no coefficient in Table 4 can be mistaken for the effect of its index condition.
  • Eleven new decisions are named, resolved, and marked for reversal.

Not settled.

  • Variance estimation. Inherited decision 10 is data-blocked. The sandwich and Kish intervals bracket the understatement from below; neither is the quantity Section 5.7 specifies. Delivering it requires Research Data Centre access.
  • Two of the nineteen conditions. “Digestive diseases” has no PUMF item, and “mental illness” is not separable from mood disorder. Neither gap is closeable from these files.
  • Section 5.9. Sex-stratified models remain outstanding. They are the natural next script, and they follow this one’s shape almost exactly: two subgroups instead of seventeen, cut on sex rather than on a condition.
  • Section 5.1. Little’s MCAR test and multiple imputation are not performed; complete-case analysis stands in, inherited from model-1 along with its cost.
  • Model adequacy inside subgroups. Whether a negative binomial is the right likelihood for a subgroup outcome that is still majority zeros is not tested here, any more than it was in model-1. Calibration, rootograms and hurdle alternatives belong to a dedicated evaluation report reading the artifacts in Step 10.

How to use this report. Model 2 is the estimation of record for Sections 5.7 and 5.8. Reports that follow should load the objects in Table t7 and interpret them; re-estimating would produce a second set of numbers with no better claim to authority and a real chance of drifting from these.
